mas11-logic.title: Statements, quantifiers and logical equivalence
mas11-logic.coverage: Lesson concept checks followed by related subject revision.

questions.prompt: Statements, quantifiers and logical equivalence — What disproves a universal assertion on its stated domain?
options: One valid counterexample.
One supporting example.
A witness proving a different existential claim.
Changing the domain without stating it.
questions.explanation: A universal claim must hold for every domain member; a single failure is decisive.

questions.prompt: Building geometric proofs from stated results — Which fact may be used in a geometric proof?
options: The desired conclusion assumed as an initial fact.
A given, definition or previously justified result whose conditions hold.
A length inferred only from the drawing scale.
A right angle silently added to a general quadrilateral.
questions.explanation: Every geometric fact in the argument needs a valid origin and applicable hypotheses.

questions.prompt: Converse, inverse, contrapositive and counterexamples — Which statement is logically equivalent to $P\Rightarrow Q$?
options: $\neg P\Rightarrow\neg Q$.
$P\Rightarrow\neg Q$.
$\neg Q\Rightarrow\neg P$.
$Q\Rightarrow P$.
questions.explanation: The contrapositive preserves the truth conditions of the original implication.

questions.prompt: Cyclic quadrilaterals, equal chords and converses — What additional condition permits the supplementary-opposite-angle theorem?
options: Only that the total angle sum is 360 degrees.
That two sides look horizontal.
That every chord is a diameter.
The quadrilateral is cyclic in the appropriate configuration.
questions.explanation: All four vertices must lie on one circle for the forward theorem.

questions.prompt: Semicircles, central angles and equal-arc angles — What central angle must be used when a circumference angle intercepts the major arc?
options: The reflex central angle for that major arc.
Always the smaller central angle.
The tangent angle regardless of endpoints.
Any angle measured from the drawing.
questions.explanation: The central and circumference angles must subtend the same identified arc.

questions.prompt: Intersecting chords and multi-step circle proofs — What geometric bound applies when a chord of length 13 is divided into x and 13-x?
options: The two lengths must always be equal.
$x$ can be any real number.
Only $x>13$ is allowed.
questions.explanation: Both segments must be positive, so the total imposes upper and lower bounds.

questions.prompt: Alternate segments and tangent–secant lengths — Which two secant lengths occur in $MT^2=MA\times MB$?
options: The tangent and the near distance with no square.
Any two visible segments.
The near and full distances measured from external point M.
Only the internal chord and the circle radius.
questions.explanation: Both secant factors start at the external point, so the full length includes the internal chord.

questions.prompt: Proof by contradiction and rigorous conclusions — What must a contradiction proof show?
options: One supportive numerical example.
An impossible result after division by zero.
That a stronger unrelated assertion is false.
The negation of the conclusion leads to an impossibility using valid steps.
questions.explanation: The negated conclusion must be the assumption ruled out, and the chain must remain valid.

questions.prompt: Vector addition, subtraction and scalar multiples — What does multiplying a nonzero vector by a negative scalar do?
options: Reverses direction and scales magnitude by the scalar’s absolute value.
Makes the magnitude negative.
Always gives a perpendicular vector.
Changes only one component.
questions.explanation: All components scale together; magnitude remains nonnegative.

questions.prompt: Rhombus diagonals and midpoint-parallelogram proofs — Which hypothesis is essential for perpendicular diagonals to characterise a rhombus in this theorem?
options: The drawing is symmetric on the page.
The figure is a nondegenerate parallelogram.
It is any quadrilateral whatsoever.
One diagonal happens to be horizontal.
questions.explanation: The vector identity uses parallelogram adjacent sides and their resulting diagonal expressions.

questions.prompt: Directed vectors, components and unit vectors — How is $\overrightarrow{AB}$ obtained from position vectors?
options: The sum of both magnitudes only.
Always a positive pair of components.
Position of B minus position of A.
Position of A minus position of B.
questions.explanation: Displacement is endpoint minus start and retains signed direction.

questions.prompt: Scalar and vector projections — Which denominator occurs in vector projection onto nonzero b?
options: $|\mathbf b|$ while still multiplying by b.
Zero regardless of direction.
$|\mathbf a|^2$ in every case.
$|\mathbf b|^2$.
questions.explanation: The vector projection coefficient multiplies b, so its denominator is b’s squared magnitude.

questions.prompt: Repeated objects and avoiding duplicate counts — Why divide by $3!$ for three indistinguishable As in a complete arrangement?
options: Their internal relabellings leave the visible arrangement unchanged.
Every word must have length three.
The three As are three different colours.
All positions are unordered committees.
questions.explanation: Each visible arrangement would be counted 3! times if the identical As were artificially labelled.

questions.prompt: Two-set and three-set inclusion–exclusion — Why add the triple intersection in the three-set union formula?
options: All categories are disjoint.
Triple members would otherwise have net count zero.
The triple is not part of any pairwise intersection.
Every member of the universe belongs to the triple.
questions.explanation: Three initial inclusions and three pairwise subtractions leave zero, so adding once restores the required count.

questions.prompt: Dot product, angles and perpendicularity — What type of object is a dot product?
options: A two-component displacement.
An angle with no additional calculation.
A scalar.
Always a unit vector.
questions.explanation: The dot product is a number that relates magnitudes and the cosine of an angle.

questions.prompt: Addition, multiplication and factorial counting — When do mutually exclusive alternatives use addition?
options: Whenever all alternatives are selected in sequence.
Whenever alternatives overlap with no correction.
Only when every category has equal size.
When exactly one of the nonoverlapping alternatives is chosen.
questions.explanation: Nonoverlapping cases partition the outcomes, so their counts add.

questions.prompt: Pigeonhole reasoning and guaranteed outcomes — What count forces at least r+1 objects in one of k boxes?
options: $kr$ always.
$k+r$ in every situation.
One object regardless of r.
questions.explanation: If every box had at most r objects, total capacity would be kr.

questions.prompt: Restricted permutations and block methods — Why is the internal factor 2 used for an adjacent block of two distinct objects?
options: The block always occupies two fixed positions.
They can occur in either order inside the block.
The entire line must be divided by two.
Each object is indistinguishable.
questions.explanation: The outer arrangement treats the block as one unit; its two internal orders remain distinct.

questions.prompt: Combinations, restrictions and Pascal identities — Which change turns a committee-selection problem into an ordered-assignment problem?
options: Writing the committee in a different list order without changing its membership.
Choosing the complement of a committee.
Giving selected members distinct roles.
Using distinct people but no roles.
questions.explanation: Distinct roles make swapping members produce a different outcome.

questions.prompt: Displacement, velocity and force models — Which quantity defines average velocity?
options: Total distance divided by time.
The unweighted average of any two speed readings.
The sum of force magnitudes.
Net displacement divided by total elapsed time.
questions.explanation: Velocity is directed; distance/time instead defines average speed.

questions.prompt: Complex quadratic roots and linear factors — When must a nonreal root occur with its conjugate?
options: When the polynomial has real coefficients.
For every polynomial with any complex coefficients.
Only when the polynomial is monic.
Only when the root has modulus 1.
questions.explanation: Real coefficients make conjugation preserve the polynomial equation.

questions.prompt: Induction for divisibility and its logical limits — Which completes a divisibility induction step?
options: Giving a calculator approximation.
Writing the next expression as the divisor times an integer.
Checking only the next numerical example.
Assuming the desired next expression is divisible.
questions.explanation: Divisibility is an exact integer statement, established for arbitrary k.

questions.prompt: Mathematical induction for sums — What is added when extending $\sum_{j=1}^k j^2$ to k+1 terms?
options: Nothing; just change the notation.
questions.explanation: The new upper limit introduces the square of the next integer.

questions.prompt: Irrationality and contradiction with reduced fractions — Why is lowest terms specified in the standard irrationality proof?
options: To require numerator and denominator both positive.
To make all fractions irrational.
To avoid squaring.
To make a common factor in numerator and denominator a contradiction.
questions.explanation: Without coprimality, even numerator and denominator would not contradict the fraction representation.

questions.prompt: Determinants, inverses and singular matrices — When does a $2\times2$ real matrix have an inverse?
options: When its determinant is nonzero.
Whenever all four entries are nonzero.
Only when its determinant is positive.
Whenever it is square, without another condition.
questions.explanation: Both positive and negative nonzero determinants allow inversion; zero does not.

questions.prompt: Matrix notation, arithmetic and compatible dimensions — When is matrix addition defined?
options: Only when every entry is positive.
When the matrices have identical row and column counts.
Whenever they have the same total number of entries.
Whenever the first column count equals the second row count.
questions.explanation: Addition compares corresponding positions; equal total size alone does not guarantee matching shapes.

questions.prompt: Dilations, rotations, reflections and translations — What do the columns of a plane transformation matrix represent?
options: The translation vector for any affine transformation.
The two original coordinate axes only.
The images of the two standard basis vectors.
The images of every point at once without multiplication.
questions.explanation: Linearity determines the image of any vector from its two basis components.

questions.prompt: Reciprocal functions, domains and asymptotes — Where does $\csc x$ have vertical asymptotes?
options: Only where sine is 1.
At every angle.
Only at cosine’s zeros.
At $x=k\pi$.
questions.explanation: Cosecant is the reciprocal of sine, so sine zeros determine its singularities.

questions.prompt: Matrix equations and two-variable systems — What does a zero coefficient determinant tell you about a two-variable linear system?
options: It has no unique solution; consistency must still be checked.
It always has no solutions.
It always has infinitely many solutions.
It has exactly one solution at the origin.
questions.explanation: Proportional coefficient rows may describe either coincident or distinct parallel lines.

questions.prompt: Determinants, area scaling and orientation — What is the geometric area scale for determinant -4?
options: Zero because the determinant is negative.
4, with orientation reversed.
-4 square units.
2, with orientation preserved.
questions.explanation: Absolute determinant determines area magnitude; its sign determines orientation.

questions.prompt: Proving and applying compound and double angles — What sign occurs in $\cos(A-B)$ between the two products?
options: No second product.
A sign determined by calculator rounding.
A plus sign.
Always a minus sign.
questions.explanation: Cosine’s compound identity uses the opposite sign to the angle combination.

questions.prompt: Transformed sine, cosine and tangent graphs — What is the amplitude of $-4\sin(3x)+2$?
questions.explanation: Amplitude is the absolute value of the sine coefficient; the sign controls reflection.

questions.prompt: Pythagorean, product-to-sum and derived identities — What restriction survives simplifying $\sin^2x/(1-\cos x)$?
options: $\cos x\ne1$.
No restriction because cancellation always extends equality everywhere.
Only $\sin x=1$.
All x are excluded.
questions.explanation: Cancellation preserves equivalence only where the original denominator is nonzero.

questions.prompt: Matrix products, order and identity — What determines entry $(AB)_{ij}$?
options: The sum of all entries.
Row i of A dotted with column j of B.
Entry $a_{ij}$ times entry $b_{ij}$.
Column i of A dotted with row j of B.
questions.explanation: Multiplication combines a row of the left factor with a column of the right.

questions.prompt: All trigonometric solutions and transformed intervals — Why translate the x interval when solving $\sin(2x)=c$?
options: The factor 2 never affects periodicity.
Only the first quadrant can contain solutions.
The transformed angle can span more cycles than x.
Inverse sine automatically lists every branch.
questions.explanation: Complete solutions require every transformed-angle branch inside the transformed interval.

questions.prompt: Auxiliary-angle forms and periodic modelling — Why must alpha’s quadrant be checked in coefficient matching?
options: Every phase must be acute.
Amplitude can always be chosen negative without a phase convention.
The period determines the signs of every coefficient.
An inverse tangent ratio alone can lose the signs of sine and cosine.
questions.explanation: Both matched coefficient signs identify the correct phase quadrant.
